lesson.title: Read a vector

steps.headline: Directions as a pair of numbers

lead.text: Start with the café, 4 blocks east and 1 block north of where you stand. On a map east runs across the page and north runs up it, so the café's directions are 4 across and 1 up. Every direction of this kind has the same two parts, which means we can drop the words and keep the numbers: (4, 1). The first number says how far across to go and the second says how far up.

Each number in the pair is called a coordinate. We name them with letters: the across number is x and the up number is y, so in (4, 1) we have x = 4 and y = 1. A pair of numbers written in a fixed order like this is called a vector. You can picture it as an arrow that starts where you stand and ends at the café.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows the café's vector and, for comparison, a library at (2, 3). Switch between them and watch where each arrow ends. Across always comes first and up always comes second, so reading a vector comes down to knowing which position you are looking at.

lead.text: The café is at (4, 1), as before. A bank is at (1, 4), which means 1 block east and 4 blocks north. Both are measured from where you stand.

reveal.text: The café's across number is 4 and the bank's is 1. Only the first numbers describe east and west, so those are the ones to compare.

lead.text: So far every number has been positive, because the café lies east and north of you. Places do not always lie that way. A kiosk might be 3 blocks west of you and 2 blocks north. Rather than invent new words, we put a minus sign on the number: a negative across number means left, and a negative up number means down.

The kiosk is at (−3, 2). Its x coordinate is −3, which is 3 to the left, and its y coordinate is 2, which is 2 up. A fountain 5 blocks east and 1 block south would be (5, −1), because south is down and down is negative.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the kiosk's arrow starts at the same corner as before and heads left as it climbs. The sign belongs to the number it sits in front of. It does not change which position the number is in, so the first number is still x and the second is still y, whatever their signs.

steps.headline: Read the vector (−4, 1): what are x and y?

workedSteps.text: The pair is written (x, y), so x is the first number. Its minus sign stays with it, so x means 4 to the left.
y is the second number. It has no minus sign, so it means 1 up.

lead.text: Decide which of the two numbers the question asks about before you answer, and keep its sign if it has one.

reveal.text: You read x straight from the first position. The −2 is y, and it sends the arrow down.

lead.text: Take the pairs (2, 6) and (6, 2). They use the same two numbers, yet (2, 6) means 2 across and 6 up, and (6, 2) means 6 across and 2 up. One ends high above the starting point and the other ends far along to the side. Two vectors are the same only when their coordinates match in every position, so swapping the numbers gives a different vector.

A pair can also hold a zero. The pair (5, 0) goes 5 across and no distance up, so it runs along the ground. A zero in a position means there is no movement in that direction. A pair that is zero in both positions has a name of its own, the zero vector, and it is written (0, 0).

workedSteps.text: Compare the x coordinates, then the y coordinates. Are the vectors the same?

lead.text: Read each number as an instruction, the way you read the café's directions.

reveal.text: You read each zero as an instruction to stay put. Zero across and zero up is no movement at all, so the zero vector marks the starting point itself.

lead.text: So far each pair has been the address of a place, measured from where you stand. A vector has a second use: it can describe a move, a change from wherever you happen to be. The directions 'go 3 across and 4 up' make sense from any corner of the grid, and they always add the same 3 and 4 to wherever you started.

A robot on a factory floor shows the idea. Its controller sends a move such as (3, 4), and the robot reads it exactly as you read the café's directions: the first number is how far across and the second is how far up. A robot that starts somewhere else follows the same move and ends somewhere else, but the move itself stays the same.
Seen this way a vector is an instruction about a change. That is why two of them can be put one after the other to make a single longer move, which the next lesson works out.
A factory robot is told its next move as a vector (across, up). The move (2, 5) would send it 2 across and 5 up.

lesson.orientation: Read signed coordinates and distinguish vectors from individual scalars.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You are standing in a town laid out on a grid, and a friend asks how to reach a café. You could draw a map, or you could say 'walk 4 blocks east, then 1 block north'. Directions like that carry everything your friend needs, and the same style of directions describes how a boat is steered or how a character moves across a game screen.

Writing them out takes a lot of words. A bank 1 block east and 4 blocks north needs another sentence, and a delivery driver might need fifty. Mathematicians shortened directions to a pair of numbers, and that pair is one of the simplest objects in linear algebra, the subject of this course.
This lesson shows how to read such a pair. We begin with the café, learn what each number says, work out what a minus sign does, and finish by seeing why the order of the two numbers matters.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a pair of directions with its signs and say why swapping the two numbers gives a different place.

recap.keyIdea: A vector is an ordered list of coordinates: across first, then up. Swap the numbers and you have a different vector.

blocks.text: Back at the café, you can now give its directions as two numbers. You read x and y from pairs with minus signs, showed that (1, 4) and (4, 1) are different vectors, and saw that the zero vector leaves you where you began.

recap.nextHook: A vector is a move, so two moves can follow one another. The next lesson starts with a walk of two legs and works out where it ends.
